question: Information has come to light regarding the possible expansion of the Astravets Nuclear Power Plant, including plans to build a third reactor and develop new nuclear-related facilities, such as a radioactive waste storage facility. These plans raise serious concerns regarding the transparency of their implementation and their compliance with international safety and environmental standards.

Lithuania and other countries in the region have repeatedly pointed out that Belarus systematically fails to comply with the requirements of the Espoo Convention, drags its feet or fails to provide detailed responses to questions from neighbouring countries, and that some decisions regarding hazardous facilities are potentially adopted even before official environmental impact assessment procedures have been conducted.
In light of the foregoing: 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of Belarus’s plans to expand the Astravets NPP and construct new nuclear energy facilities, given its previous violations of international obligations?
What specific actions does the Commission intend to take at EU level to ensure that such projects are not implemented in violation of the Espoo Convention and other international safety standards?

Would the Commission consider additional political, economic or sanction-based measures to halt the expansion of the Astravets NPP until all safety concerns raised by EU experts and neighbouring countries have been fully addressed?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The Commission understands the concerns of the Honourable Member regarding the safety of the Astravets nuclear power plant. Given the current political situation, all bilateral relations with the authorities of Russia and Belarus have been suspended.

The European Nuclear Safety Regulators Group (ENSREG) completed a peer review of the post-Fukushima nuclear safety assessment ‘stress tests’ of the Astravets nuclear power plant in 2021 and issued safety improvement recommendations. The nuclear safety regulator of Belarus drew up a National Action Plan, updated in 20231, to implement these recommendations.

The Commission continues to monitor Belarus’s progress in implementing the remaining safety improvement recommendations within the framework of relevant multilateral conventions adopted under the auspices the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), but it is not currently in a position to restart direct contacts with the Belarus authorities.

The Commission, alongside and in support of the most impacted Member States follows closely the relevant developments also under the framework of the Convention on Environmental Impact Assessment in a Transboundary Context and the Protocol on Strategic Environmental Assessment (Espoo Convention and its Protocol).
The Commission will continue to maintain contacts with the IAEA, which has the mandate to promote the implementation of international nuclear safety standards worldwide, including in Belarus.

The Commission uses as well existing international peer review mechanisms, notably during the 10th Review Meeting of the Convention on Nuclear Safety in April 2026, to probe the implementation by Belarus of its obligations under this Convention.
